name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,124

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Get on very well with old charmer?

blocks.note: to prosper is to get on very well, to thrive
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Someone hits it off splendidly with an elderly smooth-talker.
explanation.walkthrough: PROSPERO is the magician of Shakespeare's The Tempest, whose spells charm the island's visitors.
explanation.definitionFit: Prospero is a magician, and a charmer in the old sense is one who casts spells or enchantments.

clue.text: Places where Shakespeare may have got paid?

definitions.text: Places where Shakespeare may have got paid?

blocks.clueFragment: Places where Shakespeare may have got paid?
blocks.note: surface reading: the theatres or patrons that paid a playwright for his work

blocks.clueFragment: Places where Shakespeare may have got paid?
blocks.note: setter's reading: the short name for publishing houses, which pay an author, and also taverns, many of them named after the Bard

explanation.surface: A literary historian wonders where the Bard collected his fees.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is short for publishers, but it is also the everyday word for taverns, and The Shakespeare is a common British pub name.
explanation.definitionFit: Publishers pay writers for books, and the four-letter informal abbreviation for publishing firms doubles as the word for drinking houses.

clue.text: Work involving a dustman– someone we all like

blocks.note: first meaning: the Dickens novel whose plot turns on Mr Boffin, the Golden Dustman
second meaning: a person known and liked by both or all of us

explanation.surface: A job on the bin lorry, done by a refuse collector everybody is fond of.
explanation.walkthrough: A dustman is a British rubbish collector; Dickens's last finished novel is built around a fortune made from dust heaps.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both the title of a Dickens novel about dust-heap wealth and a description of a friend shared by several people.

clue.text: Rustic friend hosting Byatt, initially, then Hill

indicators.note: a host takes guests in, so the word for friend holds what follows inside it

blocks.note: a pal is a friend
the novelist A. S. Byatt's initials
a tor is a rocky hill, especially on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A country companion entertains the novelist Byatt and then the novelist Hill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' here means her initials, A. S., rather than just her first letter. Susan Hill is a novelist too, but here Hill is just a hill.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastoral describes country life and rural scenes, so it is a synonym for rustic as an adjective.

clue.text: Some author hindering Scottish antiquarian…

indicators.note: some of the following words means only a part of their letters is wanted, taken in a run

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the end of author and the start of hindering

explanation.surface: A writer is getting in the way of a Scottish antiquary.
explanation.walkthrough: Alexander Henry Rhind was a Victorian Scottish antiquarian, remembered for the Rhind mathematical papyrus.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhind was a Scottish collector and student of ancient artefacts, which is exactly what an antiquarian is.

clue.text: NY actor associated with good books

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
OT, the Old Testament, is the usual crossword source for books
a ham is an overacting performer

explanation.surface: A New York performer is linked with some fine literature.
explanation.walkthrough: The actor comes last in the answer though first in the clue: the good books are joined after him.
explanation.definitionFit: Gotham is a long-standing nickname for New York City, popularised by Washington Irving and later by Batman comics.

clue.text: … bent over first two pieces of Euripides’ work

indicators.note: something bent is twisted out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
the opening pair of letters of the following name is all that is used

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening two letters of the Greek playwright's name

explanation.surface: Continuing from the antiquarian, someone stoops over the opening pages of Euripides' writings.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links the surface to 4 down, but the wordplay stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Oeuvre is a borrowed French term for a single artistic work or an author's whole body of writing.

clue.text: Fry thanks readers of turn of the century book

indicators.note: frying cooks and changes food, so the letters that follow are reworked

blocks.note: every letter of these three words is used

explanation.surface: Stephen Fry expresses gratitude to the readers of a book.
explanation.walkthrough: Fry looks like the actor and writer Stephen Fry, but it is the instruction to cook up the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Conrad's novella was serialised in 1899 and published in 1902, so it straddles the turn of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Way to support major satirical Lewis novel

indicators.note: in a down entry, what supports something sits beneath it, so the first word goes below the second

blocks.note: main means chief or major
a street is a way or road

explanation.surface: A road is built to hold up a big satirical novel by Lewis.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis is Sinclair Lewis, whose 1920 novel mocks small-town Midwestern life.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinclair Lewis's novel Main Street satirises the narrow conformity of a small American town.

clue.text: No arcane drunk, this poet of love and wine

definitions.text: this poet of love and wine

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about, so the letters before it stagger out of order

blocks.note: every letter of these two words is used

explanation.surface: A tipsy poet celebrating love and wine is hardly an obscure one.
explanation.walkthrough: Drunk suits the surface perfectly, since the poet in question sang of wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Anacreon was an ancient Greek lyric poet famous for drinking songs and erotic verse.

clue.text: No time for Bad Vibrations author

indicators.note: having no time for something means dropping the abbreviation for time
something bad has gone wrong, so the remaining letters are disordered

blocks.note: taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time, and it is removed

explanation.surface: A writer has no patience with the Beach Boys' Good Vibrations turned bad.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface plays on the Beach Boys' song Good Vibrations.
explanation.definitionFit: Boris Vian was a French novelist, poet and jazz musician, author of L'Écume des jours.

clue.text: A Taste of Honey? No, Green Tea!

blocks.clueFragment: A Taste of Honey? No, Green Tea!
blocks.note: surface reading: someone corrects the title of Shelagh Delaney's play, swapping in a drink

blocks.clueFragment: A Taste of Honey? No, Green Tea!
blocks.note: setter's reading: the savoury taste is not that of honey, which is sweet, but the one green tea is prized for

explanation.surface: Someone misremembers the title of Shelagh Delaney's play A Taste of Honey.
explanation.walkthrough: The fifth basic taste, alongside sweet, sour, salt and bitter, is the savoury one found in green tea, seaweed and broth.
explanation.definitionFit: Umami is the Japanese name for the savoury basic taste, strong in green tea and absent from sweet honey.

clue.text: Romantic display of affection and love

blocks.note: a hug is a physical display of affection
love is nil in tennis, written as O

explanation.surface: A romantic shows affection and love.
explanation.walkthrough: Romantic with a capital R means a writer of the Romantic movement, not a sentimental person.
explanation.definitionFit: Victor Hugo was a leading figure of French Romanticism in literature.

clue.text: “Judges don’t age. Time— them” (Enid Bagnold)

blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation with its verb blanked out
setter's reading: the missing word is the verb from Bagnold's play The Chalk Garden, meaning that time adorns judges rather than ageing them

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: the solver supplies the missing word from Enid Bagnold's play The Chalk Garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Time adorns judges with dignity instead of ageing them, so the missing verb means embellishes or honours.

clue.text: 1948 sci-fi book by Heinlein or William Burroughs?

blocks.note: first meaning: Robert Heinlein's juvenile novel about a young recruit to a space patrol
second meaning: slang for a dreamy, drug-addled person, which fits the heroin-using Beat writer

explanation.surface: A quiz asks who wrote a 1948 science fiction novel: Heinlein or William Burroughs?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks Burroughs as an example: a famously drug-fogged writer is a fair instance of the slang term.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a Heinlein title and also slang for someone vague and out of touch, often from drugs.

clue.text: He wrote 20 supernatural works (after leaving navy)

indicators.note: works in the sense of operates on, so the letters of the word before it are worked into a new order
after something has left, it is gone, so the abbreviation for the navy is taken out first

blocks.note: taken as written
RN is the Royal Navy, and these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A writer produced twenty books about the paranormal once he quit the navy.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 is a cross-reference to 20 across, the novel Moon Palace; 'works' looks like a noun but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Auster, the American novelist of The New York Trilogy, published Moon Palace in 1989.

clue.text: Squeal about Arthur, say, and his sort of life

definitions.note: adjective as in the sporting life; 'his' refers to the fighter in Arthur, a port

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for squeal wraps the next piece

blocks.note: to sing is slang for squealing, informing to the police
Port Arthur is an example of a port

explanation.surface: Someone informs on a man called Arthur and his way of living.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arthur, say' points to Port Arthur, so Arthur stands for a harbour. To sing is underworld slang for squealing to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: A sporting life is one devoted to games, hunting or gambling, so the adjective describes that kind of existence.

clue.text: “Seek not for fresher founts—, Just drop your bucket where you are” (Sam Walter Foss)

definitions.text: “Seek not for fresher founts—, Just drop your bucket where you are” (Sam Walter Foss)

blocks.clueFragment: “Seek not for fresher founts—, Just drop your bucket where you are”
blocks.note: surface reading: a couplet with a word blanked out
setter's reading: the missing word comes from the American poet's homely verse, meaning at a great distance

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: the solver completes the line from Sam Walter Foss, an American poet of folksy verse.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem advises against searching distant places for water, so the missing word means far away or at a distance.

clue.text: Fugitive upsetting wig in The Trial?

indicators.note: upsetting knocks something over, so the letters of the hairpiece are jumbled
in places the jumbled word inside the word for a trial

blocks.note: a trial is a contest or test, as in a trial match; 'The' completes the Kafka title
taken as written

explanation.surface: A runaway causes uproar by knocking off a judge's wig during Kafka's The Trial.
explanation.walkthrough: The Trial looks like Kafka's novel, but it is just a trial, a contest.
explanation.definitionFit: Abel Magwitch is the escaped convict in Dickens's Great Expectations, a fugitive from the hulks.

clue.text: In which Fanny Hill was laid down to flog, I’m told

definitions.text: In which Fanny Hill was laid down

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it, so the word is taken by sound rather than spelling

blocks.note: to flog is British slang for to sell

explanation.surface: A smutty question about where the heroine Fanny Hill was put to bed to be whipped.
explanation.walkthrough: John Cleland wrote Fanny Hill while in debtors' prison, so the book was laid down, written, in a prison room; the surface invites a racier reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleland composed the novel while confined in the Fleet Prison, so its place of writing was a prison room.

clue.text: Novel way to show cheek to Buckingham?

blocks.note: to moon is to bare one's buttocks, showing one's cheeks
Buckingham Palace is the monarch's London residence

explanation.surface: A cheeky suggestion for insulting the royal household.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheek means both impudence and a buttock; mooning shows the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Moon Palace is a 1989 novel by Paul Auster, the answer at 15 across.

clue.text: Retired editor punching stern TLS solver?

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so the abbreviation is read backwards
a punch goes into something, so this piece is driven inside the next

blocks.note: ED is the abbreviation for editor
the stern is the rear of a ship

explanation.surface: A cross editor takes a swing at a stern TLS crossword fan.
explanation.walkthrough: Stern looks like an adjective for a severe person, but it is the back end of a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone who reads the Times Literary Supplement, its crossword solvers included, is one of its readership.

clue.text: Erotically macabre author pulling writer in Peter Street?

indicators.note: pulling a thing in takes it inside, so the author's name holds the next word

blocks.note: Angela Carter wrote dark, erotic fairy tales such as The Bloody Chamber
a pen is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: A sexy gothic novelist picks up a writer in a street.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Street looks like an address but is a man: the master carpenter who built the Globe Theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Street was the Elizabethan builder who constructed the Globe and Fortune theatres, a woodworking trade.

clue.text: Royal undone by poison ultimately

indicators.note: being undone by something means losing out to it, so a letter is ousted by another
ultimately means finally, so only the closing letter of the word is used

blocks.note: regal means royal
the final letter of poison

explanation.surface: A princess meets her end through poison.
explanation.walkthrough: The last letter of the word for royal is undone and replaced by the last of poison. In King Lear, Regan dies after Goneril poisons her.
explanation.definitionFit: Lear's daughter Regan, a princess, is poisoned by her sister Goneril, so the whole clue describes her fate.

clue.text: Pans books that lack a middle section

indicators.note: lacking a middle means the central letter of the word is missing

blocks.note: an author's works are books

explanation.surface: A critic slates books that sag in the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: Pans looks like a verb for a harsh review, but it is a noun for cooking vessels.
explanation.definitionFit: A wok is a deep round-bottomed frying pan used in Chinese cooking, so the plural matches pans.

clue.text: Greek creating discord upset father

indicators.note: in a down entry, upset means turned upside down, so the word reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: to sire is to father, and a sire is a father

explanation.surface: A Greek stirs up a quarrel and upsets his father.
explanation.definitionFit: Eris is the Greek goddess of strife, who caused the Trojan War with the golden apple of discord.

clue.text: Fear a street judge in hearing

indicators.note: in hearing means as heard by the ear, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: Judge Dredd is the comic-strip lawman who dispenses justice on the streets

explanation.surface: Someone is frightened of a judge holding a hearing about a street.
explanation.walkthrough: Judge Dredd, of the British comic 2000 AD, is judge, jury and executioner on the streets of Mega-City One.
explanation.definitionFit: Dread is great fear or apprehension, a synonym as a noun.

clue.text: Nearly time to put on Dent’s underclothes?

blocks.note: nigh means nearly
T is the abbreviation for time
to wear clothes is to put them on

explanation.surface: It is almost time to put on the underwear of someone named Dent.
explanation.walkthrough: Dent is Arthur Dent of The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, who crosses the galaxy in his dressing gown.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Dent spends the story in his dressing gown and pyjamas, garments for sleeping in.

clue.text: Members of House in The Stud or Score!

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the run of words that follows

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of Stud, all of or and the start of Score

explanation.surface: Members of a family appear in Jackie Collins's racy novel The Stud, or in a celebration of a goal.
explanation.walkthrough: House means a royal dynasty, as in the House of Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tudors were the royal dynasty, the House of Tudor, that ruled England from 1485 to 1603.

clue.text: Wild Hessian heading for Crane, an immortal lover?

definitions.note: read as the lover of an immortal

indicators.note: something wild is unruly, so the letters are thrown into disorder
a heading is what comes on top, so only the opening letter of the name is taken

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of Crane

explanation.surface: A crazed Hessian soldier heads for Ichabod Crane, as in The Legend of Sleepy Hollow.
explanation.walkthrough: In Irving's tale the Headless Horseman is a Hessian soldier and Ichabod Crane his quarry. Anchises was mortal, but loved by a goddess.
explanation.definitionFit: Anchises was the Trojan prince loved by the goddess Aphrodite, making him the mortal lover of an immortal.
